Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
  • You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf.
  • While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.

Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.

It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add notable dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a newly introduced activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.

There’s also a work-focused version, which the firm explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”.

It has been revealed that the personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.

Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.

In a recent development, caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone consumers and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Industry observers note that comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.

Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies owners and recommends the next steps.

It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.

Comma is free to start and open source.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized strategy.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

It has been revealed that the tech giant rolled out in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is right now free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.

One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.

Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.

Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.

Sources indicate that according to the firm, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”.

Notably, the manufacturer envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.

It has been revealed that currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.

Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

Recent findings suggest that the always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. People can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The organization indicates early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

The company remains in private beta.

Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.

Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of consumers by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.

It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

Industry observers note that it can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.

The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.

Industry observers note that it’s right now in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month,  20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.

Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Customers can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.

Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

It has been revealed that users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and looks. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.

It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

Sources indicate that it works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.

Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.

Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Recent findings suggest that owners can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of aims, receipts, dates, files, and other details.

In a recent development, there’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.

Poke introduced in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent tech giant The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

In a recent development, rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.

Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

Rene is presently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Instead of waiting for people to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.

Recent findings suggest that the company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet unveiled a public release date.

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

It has been revealed that for instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and blueprint from scratch.

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. People can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.

According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.

Tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.

According to recent reports, the company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.

The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.

The basic blueprint starts at $19.99 per month.

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives people a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.

In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that debuted an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

According to recent reports, A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials.

Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo indicates it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.

Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

It displays images from Amazon Photos, which supports uploads from both iOS and Android devices, including photos stored in iCloud. You can choose which people or albums to display, or let Alexa Plus do the work, which often results in photos based on your facial expression, the season, and even the lighting. You can also search for specific photos with voice commands, letting you easily pull up images of your first dog, your child as a baby, and other shots without having to scroll endlessly through years of photos yourself.

If you want to add a more personal touch, Amazon also lets you attach voice notes to individual photos via the Amazon Photos app. For example, you can add a recording of your kid explaining their Halloween costume to a trick-or-treating photo. Plus, you can preload the frame with photos and recordings before gifting it, so your loved one won’t have to spend time setting it up.

We’re still testing Amazon’s answer to the Aura frame, but it looks like a particularly good option if you’re already an Amazon Prime member. A Prime subscription grants you unlimited full-resolution photo storage and access to Alexa Plus at no additional cost, and unlike Amazon’s smart displays, the frame doesn’t serve up annoying ads. That mentioned, you don’t need a subscription to use it, and new customers can always access a limited-time trial of Alexa Plus.

This is the title for the native ad.

#58697. Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (876 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, "The threat is immense," said Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference  recently.
  • Recent findings suggest that it was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member statesto reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added.
  • A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, mentioned Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, "The threat is immense," said Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference  recently. "An estimated cumulative number of 39 million deaths directly attributable to AMR [antimicrobial resistance] would occur in the next 25 years.".

Recent findings suggest that it was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member statesto reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added. "When we see the trend, the investments, the action, we don't think we are on the right track.".

A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, mentioned Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen. "If antibiotics were no longer effective, modern medicine as we know it today would no longer be possible at all.".

Imirzalioglu is not only an expert on antibiotic resistance but also on "One Health," a concept adopted in 2004 by experts in human medicine, veterinary medicine and nature conservation. It recognizes that the health of humans, animals and the environment is closely interconnected.

After all, antibiotics and antimicrobial-resistant germs are not just a problem in hospitals. They can also be found in animal shelters, in animal products, in waste water, in fertilizers and in plants. "One Health tries to keep an eye on all of this," Imirzalioglu stated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that for hospitals and doctors' offices this means that antibiotics must be used as selectively and purposefully as possible. To this end, research is focused primarily on developing better and faster diagnostic methods.

In a recent development, in Germany, antibiotics were frequently prescribed against respiratory or urinary tract infections, Imirzalioglu stated. But antibiotics are only effective against bacteria. If a virus causes the infection, they are ineffective.

In a recent development, nonetheless, every antibiotics dose has consequences: it damages our gut microbiome. This consists of billions of micro-organisms, primarily bacteria, which are essential for digestion, metabolism and the immune system. "If we damage the [bacteria], resistant pathogens can spread and take their place," Imirzalioglu said.

Another problem was that such a spreading of resistant pathogens in the gut often went unnoticed and without causing symptoms, he added.

So people became "carriers of resistant pathogens, which they, in turn, release back into their environment.".

Sources indicate that in this way, resistant pathogens make their way out of hospitals via toilets and sinks into wastewater and, from there, into the Baltic Sea, where they are ingested by wild birds. This pathway was traced in a study by Katharina Schaufler, a veterinarian and microbiologist at the Helmholtz Institute for One Health (HIOH).

Antibiotics have not only been used in humans on a large scale over a long time, excessive use in veterinary medicine has also led to resistance to nearly all available antibiotics, Schaufler mentioned.

It has been revealed that in 2006, an EU-wide ban on the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in animal feedcame into effect. Since then, antibiotics may only be applied as part of veterinary treatment.

The problem is that due to factory farming the use of antibiotics for medical purposes is a permanent necessity. The mere fact that animals live together in confined spaces causes infections to spread rapidly.

Lack of space as well as boredom lead the animals to injure each other and this happens in an environment where, in Schaufler's words, "there's already a high level of bacterial pressure.".

Industry observers note that through fertilizers, antibiotic-resistant pathogens enter the environment. "It has been proven that, for example, resistant bacteria can still be found on lettuce heads," the veterinarian noted. Resistant bacteria were also found time and again on meat.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that national solutions are also falling short. In many countries, antibiotics are still a standard additive in animal feed, Schaufler said. And in such countries, antibiotics could be obtained in drugstores without prescriptions, Imirzalioglu added. Both say that all of this makes the global fight against antibiotic resistance more difficult.

According to recent reports, political will is of the essence when it comes to combating antibiotic resistance. Imirzalioglu works at Guardian, a project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space.

The aim of the project is to prevent outbreaks of diseases caused by resistant bacteria by monitoring and analyzing wastewater in the German state of Hesse.

At EU level, Imirzalioglu is also an advisor at the Antimicrobial Resistance One Health Network. He sums up his experience with policymakers: "The experts and working groups have great ideas, and then these are often scaled back or stifled during the initial stages.".

Perhaps the lack of political will so far is one of the reasons why the WHO's Nyemazi is issuing an appeal to every individual: Preventing antibiotic resistance means preventing infections, through hygiene, regular vaccinations and doctor's appointments as well as taking medications in accordance with prescriptions.

This article was originally published in German.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds.
    • One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
    • Recent findings suggest that in west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds.

    One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

    Recent findings suggest that in west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

    Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

    According to recent reports, “These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”.

    The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

    “The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

    It has been revealed that he noted that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

    Sources indicate that in countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

    Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

    Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, noted a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”.

    She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

    Industry observers note that “Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II.

    A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

    Sources indicate that the ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

    "War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo noted. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.".

    Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

    The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

    The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

    Finland's coast guard remarked it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

    This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials stated.

    Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry mentioned a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

    A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is right now carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way.".

    Sources indicate that the Finnish Border Guard later remarked the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

    It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

    Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

    Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

    Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

    The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

    Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

    Industry News: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits.
    • Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
    • The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits.

    Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

    The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who noted they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

    The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

    The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

    The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

    According to recent reports, otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, stated: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”.

    According to recent reports, sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, remarked she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted promptly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

    “As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their newly introduced leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

    According to recent reports, the rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

    Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

    Recent findings suggest that “A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” remarked Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”.

    Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

    According to recent reports, the trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”.

    Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

    The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” stated Venter.

    A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

    Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

    We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

    On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no looks for Huang to return.

    Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.).

    Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

    It has been revealed that kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

    What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

    A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

    Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

    Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.

    Industry observers note that and again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.

    Recent findings suggest that kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.

    It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

    Sources indicate that so it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

    Sources indicate that anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

    In a recent development, it seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”.

    Recent findings suggest that so depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

    Kirsten:  Sure, never say never.

    It has been revealed that tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how rapidly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

    Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.

    Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

    Recent findings suggest that anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public organization. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

    The list of hacks hitting the US government over the last few months keeps growing.

    The list of hacks hitting the US government over the last few months keeps growing.

    Friday, it was reported that both the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI were hacked. In reporting on the FBI hack, CNN noted that this is the second such attack on the agency in the last few months, this time targeting the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which federal, state, and local law enforcement use to share information, including warrants and missing persons. President Donald Trump later confirmed the hack in an interview with Fox News. NBC first reported the USDA hack on Friday. According to Reuters:.

    While the payments ​database is the known extent ​of the intrusion so far, the former ‌officials ⁠warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety ​data and ​research on ⁠animal-borne illnesses, according to the report.

    The breaches come following a week of major outages across several sectors, including at the FAA and NSA, which the government has sought to reassure the public were not the result of a cyberattack.

    President Trump suggested that the breach of the FBI might not be an entirely bad thing, telling Fox News that, “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” and “wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?” referring to investigations into his ties to Russia.

    According to recent reports, the FBI suffered a breach, reported in late September, that allegedly compromised personal records of “all FBI employees and applicants.” This was followed by a hack of DHS, reported in October, comprising 40,000 employee records. In the wake of these major outages, the White House national cyber director, Sean Cairncross, stepped down this week.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine.
    • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
    • According to recent reports, in comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky stated the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine.

    Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, in comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky stated the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

    He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

    Industry observers note that "There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he stated.

    The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

    "If Putin used the internet, he could see that.".

    The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

    This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

    Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

    Recent findings suggest that A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

    Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

    Russia released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

    Footage indicates Ukrainian missile approach Crimean Bridge.

    Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

    "The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting noted.

    He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

    The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

    Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he noted the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

    Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

    Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys stated they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

    "Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

    Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, remarked the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

    Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

    That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

    Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

    "I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate.".

    Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions.".

    In a separate development on Saturday, Finland noted it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

    The Finnish defence ministry noted in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

    It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

    Russia has not publicly commented on the concern.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded.
    • In a recent development, multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities.
    • Recent findings suggest that coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded.

    In a recent development, multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

    Recent findings suggest that coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

    It has been revealed that nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

    In a recent development, after a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

    The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.
    • Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.
    • One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.

    Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.

    One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

    Industry observers note that before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

    Recent findings suggest that the compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”.

    Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

    According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:.

    On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

    Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Signal confirmed Friday that it’s limiting customers’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.
    • Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Signal confirmed Friday that it’s limiting customers’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

    Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”.

    “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she noted. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

    Sources indicate that signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

    That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”.
